Reasoning: After the switch is closed, the outer plate of C1 and the outer plate of C2 belong to the same external node, while the adjacent plates of C1 and C2 belong to the same middle node, so C1 and C2 are equivalent to being connected in parallel between the “middle node” and the “external node”, and finally the magnitudes of the voltages across the two capacitors are the same, denoted as V. Initially only C1 is charged, and its voltage is U, so the magnitude of the conserved charge associated with the middle node is C1U. After the switch is closed, this charge is distributed on the two parallel capacitors, so (C1 + C2)V = C1U. Given C1 = 2C2, substituting gives V = C1U/(C1 + C2) = 2C2U/(2C2 + C2) = 2U/3. Therefore the voltage across C1 becomes 2U/3.

method.method_draft: After noting from the diagram that S shorts the two outer terminals, set the joined outer rail to potential 0. Let the final potential of the middle junction between C1 and C2 be x; then both capacitors have voltage magnitude |x|, including C1. Before switching, C2 contributes no charge to the middle junction, while C1 contributes an algebraic charge of magnitude C1U on that isolated junction. Since no external source is present and the middle node is floating, its algebraic charge is conserved: C1 x + C2 x equals the initial corresponding charge C1U, up to sign convention. Hence x=C1U/(C1+C2). Substituting C1=2C2 gives x=2U/3, so the voltage across C1 is 2U/3.
